title: Management and operations
lede: The language of running a business that grows: costs, break-even, cash flow, KPIs, bottlenecks and systems. Know these and you can read any business book, pitch any lender, and run your trucks like a company.

sections.md:
## Revenue isn't profit
The single most important idea in business vocabulary:

- **Revenue** (or *gross income*, *top line*): all money coming in.
- **Gross profit**: revenue minus the **direct** costs of doing the work (fuel, tolls, driver pay).
- **Net profit** (*bottom line*): what's left after **all** costs, including overhead, interest and taxes.

A truck that grosses $20,000 a month can still **lose** money. The bottom line is the only line that pays you.

terms.def: Costs that **stay the same** no matter how much you work: truck payment, insurance, phone plan.
Costs that **rise with activity**: fuel, tolls, tires, maintenance per mile.
Ongoing costs of running the business that don't tie to one job: insurance, software, accounting, office.
The level of sales where revenue exactly covers all costs: zero profit, zero loss.
The **timing** of money in and out. A profitable business can still fail if cash comes in too late.
Gain ÷ cost. How much an investment earns relative to what it cost.
One of the few numbers you track to know if the business is healthy.
How much of your capacity you actually use. A truck sitting idle is low utilization.
The slowest step in a process, which limits everything else.
A written, step-by-step way to do a recurring task the same way every time.
Able to grow without costs or effort growing just as fast.
A plan B, prepared in advance, for when something goes wrong.

sections.md:
## Break-even, step by step
**Break-even** = fixed costs ÷ (price per unit − variable cost per unit)

The bottom part, **price − variable cost**, is the **contribution margin**: what each unit (each mile, each load) contributes toward paying the fixed costs.

*Example:* fixed costs are **$6,000 a month** (truck note, insurance, permits, phone). You earn **$2.30 per mile**, and variable costs are **$0.80 per mile** (fuel, maintenance, tolls).

- Contribution per mile: 2.30 − 0.80 = **$1.50**
- Break-even: 6,000 ÷ 1.50 = **4,000 miles a month**

Every mile below 4,000 loses money. Every mile above it is profit. That one number tells you how many loads you **must** book each month.

sections.md:
## KPIs: the dashboard
A KPI is a number that tells you the truth fast. A good business tracks **a few**, every week:

| KPI | Trucking example | Trading example |
|---|---|---|
| revenue per mile / per trade | revenue ÷ total miles | average P&L per trade |
| cost per mile / per trade | all costs ÷ miles | commissions and fees |
| utilization | % of days the truck is loaded | % of sessions with an A+ setup traded |
| quality | on-time %, claims | % of trades that followed the plan |
| risk | deadhead % | max drawdown |

*What gets measured gets managed* is a business cliché because it works. Pick the few numbers that matter, and look at them every week.

sections.title: ROI decision
sections.problem: An APU (auxiliary power unit) costs $9,000 installed. It saves about $300 a month in idle fuel. What's the payback period and first-year ROI?
steps: First-year ROI: (3,600 − 9,000) ÷ 9,000 = −60%: it hasn't paid for itself yet.
Over 5 years: 18,000 saved vs 9,000 cost → ROI = 100%.
sections.answer: **ROI depends on the time frame.** Worth it if you'll keep the truck long enough; a bad buy if you'll sell it next year.

sections.md:
## Systems that let you grow
- **SOPs** turn what's in your head into steps someone else can follow. You can't hire a dispatcher or a second driver until the job is written down.
- **Bottlenecks** limit everything. If you can only check load boards when you're not driving, **you** are the bottleneck, not the truck.
- **Scalable** work grows without your hours growing at the same rate. One truck you drive yourself isn't very scalable. A dispatch system serving five trucks is more scalable.
- **Contingency plans** are written **before** the crisis: breakdown, canceled load, a slow freight month. (A trading plan's daily loss limit is a contingency plan.)

sections.q: You can't grow past two trucks because you personally book every load. You are the…
sections.why: The slowest step limiting the whole system.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Revenue ≠ profit.** Always ask: what's left after **all** costs?
- **Profitable ≠ cash rich.** Net 30 payments can starve a profitable business of cash.
- **Too many KPIs.** Tracking 30 numbers is tracking none. Pick 3–5.
- **Forgetting fixed costs** when pricing a load. Each load must contribute its share of the truck note and insurance.

practice.hint: Find the contribution per mile first.

practice.q: Same truck: you drive 9,000 miles this month. Profit?
practice.hint: Every mile past break-even earns the contribution.

practice.q: A $12,000 upgrade saves $400/month. Payback period in months?
Which KPI set is best for a one-truck owner-operator?
options: Revenue per total mile, cost per mile, deadhead %, on-time %
practice.why: A few numbers that show profit, efficiency and service quality. Revenue alone hides costs; 30 metrics hide everything.
practice.hint: Few, and tied to profit and quality.
